(p-532) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surah al-Zukhruf

This surah is Meccan, by the consensus of the scholars.

The Exalted and Majestic says:

﴿Ha Mim﴾ ﴿By the Clear Book,﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand.﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise.﴾ ﴿Shall We then divert the reminder from you, [merely] because you are a people who transgress?﴾ ﴿And how many a prophet We sent among the former peoples.﴾ ﴿And no prophet came to them but that they used to mock him.﴾ ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might, and the example of the former peoples has passed.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Exalted in Might, the All-Knowing."﴾

The discussion of the letters has already been given at the beginning of the surahs. His saying, ﴿"Al-Kitab"﴾ [the Book], is in the genitive by the particle of oath "wa". As for ﴿"al-Mubin"﴾ [the Clear]: it may be from "abana", which has the meaning of "bana", i.e. became manifest, so it needs no object; and it may be transitive from "bana", in which case it must have an object, estimated as: "the Clear [one] regarding guidance, or the Law, or the like."

His saying, ﴿"Inna ja'alnahu"﴾ [Indeed, We have made it], means: We named it and made it. It is a report upon which the oath falls. The pronoun in ﴿"ja'alnahu"﴾ refers to ﴿"al-Kitab"﴾. ﴿"'Arabiyyan"﴾ means: in your language, so that no excuse remains for you. His saying, ﴿"la'allakum"﴾ [that you may], is an expression of hope according to human belief, i.e., when a human observer sees this act from Us, he hopes that he will understand the speech and comprehend it.

His saying, ﴿"Wa innahu"﴾ [And indeed, it], is conjoined to his saying, ﴿"Inna ja'alnahu"﴾. This second report also falls under the oath. ﴿"Umm al-Kitab"﴾ [the Mother of the Book] is the Preserved Tablet, and this contains an honouring of the Qur'an (p-533) and an elevation. The interpreters differed as to how it is in the "Mother of the Book". Qatada, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and 'Atiyya ibn Sa'id said: the entire Qur'an is in it, abrogating and abrogated, and from it Jibril (ﷺ) used to descend, and there it is "exalted, wise." The majority of people said: its mention is only in the Preserved Tablet, along with its rank, its station and its elevation in loftiness and wisdom. The majority of people read ﴿"fi Umm al-Kitab"﴾ with a damma on the hamza, while Yusuf, the governor of Iraq, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with a kasra on the hamza.

His saying, ﴿"Afanadribu"﴾ [Shall We then], means: shall We then leave? The Arabs say: "adraba 'an kadha" and "daraba" when one turns away from something and leaves it. ﴿"Al-Dhikr"﴾ [the reminder] is calling to Allah the Exalted and reminding of His punishment and warning of His retribution. Abu Salih said: "al-Dhikr" here is the punishment itself. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: "al-Dhikr" is the Qur'an. His saying, ﴿"Safhan"﴾ [diverting], is in the accusative like the accusative of ﴿"Sun'a Allah"﴾ [the work of Allah] [al-Naml: 88]. It may mean pardon and forgiveness of sin, so that it is as if He, the Exalted, says: shall We then leave off reminding you and warning you, pardoning you and forgiving your crimes, because you are a people who transgress? This does not fit. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It may also be that His saying "safhan" means "ignored", i.e., We leave it to pass by, while you are not held to account for accepting it, nor for reflecting upon it, nor are you alerted to it. This meaning is like the saying of the poet:

"The breezes pass by the dwellers of Dhu al-Ghada, ignoring them, and my heart is split that they blow."

That is, they pass by unheeded. So it is as if this meaning is: shall We leave you neglected? This is the view of Qatada and others. From the same root is Kuthayyir's saying:

"Forgiving, so you meet her only as a miser; and whoever tires of her union, she tires of it."

al-Sumayt ibn 'Amr and al-Sudusi read ﴿"Suhfan"﴾ with a damma on the sad.

Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿"in kuntum"﴾ with a kasra on the alif; it is a conditional whose answer is indicated by what precedes it. The rest, al-A'raj and Qatada read ﴿"an kuntum"﴾ with a fatha on the alif, meaning: because you are. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿"idh kuntum"﴾. The "al-israf" in the verse is disbelief and far-reaching misguidance in worshipping other than Allah the Exalted and associating partners with Him.

His saying, ﴿And how many a prophet We sent among the former peoples﴾: the verses are a consolation to Muhammad (ﷺ), his mention is an example for him, a warning for them, and a threat that they will be struck by what struck those who were stronger than them in might. "al-Awwalun" [the former] are the past nations, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud and others. The pronoun in His saying, ﴿kanu bihi yastahzi'un﴾ [they used to mock him], apparently is general, and what is meant is specific to those who mocked; otherwise there were among the former peoples those who did not mock. The pronoun in "minhum" refers to Quraysh. His saying, ﴿wa madha mathalu al-awwalin﴾ [and the example of the former peoples has passed], means: their affair and their custom passed on, and they became a lesson for the remainder of time.

His saying, ﴿And if you asked them﴾ and the verse... is the beginning of an argument against Quraysh which compels upon them a contradiction in their affair, for they acknowledge that the Creator who originated them and the heavens and the earth is Allah the Exalted, yet they worship idols and call them their gods. The required answer of Quraysh would be to say: "Allah created them." When the Exalted mentioned the meaning, the expression about Allah came as "the Exalted in Might, the All-Knowing", so that this would be a preparation for what He enumerates afterwards of His attributes, which He began to report and then cut off from the speech whose meaning He related from Quraysh.

The pronoun in ﴿"ja'alnahu"﴾ refers to ﴿"al-Kitab"﴾. ﴿"'Arabiyyan"﴾ means: in your language, so that no excuse remains for you. His saying, ﴿"la'allakum"﴾ [that you may], is an expression of hope according to human belief, i.e., when a human observer sees this act from Us, he hopes that he will understand the speech and comprehend it.

His saying, ﴿"Wa innahu"﴾ [And indeed, it], is conjoined to his saying, ﴿"Inna ja'alnahu"﴾. This second report also falls under the oath. ﴿"Umm al-Kitab"﴾ [the Mother of the Book] is the Preserved Tablet, and this contains an honouring of the Qur'an (p-533) and an elevation. The interpreters differed as to how it is in the "Mother of the Book". Qatada, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and 'Atiyya ibn Sa'id said: the entire Qur'an is in it, abrogating and abrogated, and from it Jibril (ﷺ) used to descend, and there it is "exalted, wise." The majority of people said: its mention is only in the Preserved Tablet, along with its rank, its station and its elevation in loftiness and wisdom. The majority of people read ﴿"fi Umm al-Kitab"﴾ with a damma on the hamza, while Yusuf, the governor of Iraq, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with a kasra on the hamza.

His saying, ﴿"Afanadribu"﴾ [Shall We then], means: shall We then leave? The Arabs say: "adraba 'an kadha" and "daraba" when one turns away from something and leaves it. ﴿"Al-Dhikr"﴾ [the reminder] is calling to Allah the Exalted and reminding of His punishment and warning of His retribution. Abu Salih said: "al-Dhikr" here is the punishment itself. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: "al-Dhikr" is the Qur'an. His saying, ﴿"Safhan"﴾ [diverting], is in the accusative like the accusative of ﴿"Sun'a Allah"﴾ [the work of Allah] [al-Naml: 88]. It may mean pardon and forgiveness of sin, so that it is as if He, the Exalted, says: shall We then leave off reminding you and warning you, pardoning you and forgiving your crimes, because you are a people who transgress? This does not fit. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It may also be that His saying "safhan" means "ignored", i.e., We leave it to pass by, while you are not held to account for accepting it, nor for reflecting upon it, nor are you alerted to it. This meaning is like the saying of the poet:

"The breezes pass by the dwellers of Dhu al-Ghada, ignoring them, and my heart is split that they blow."

That is, they pass by unheeded. So it is as if this meaning is: shall We leave you neglected? This is the view of Qatada and others. From the same root is Kuthayyir's saying:

"Forgiving, so you meet her only as a miser; and whoever tires of her union, she tires of it."

al-Sumayt ibn 'Amr and al-Sudusi read ﴿"Suhfan"﴾ with a damma on the sad.

Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿"in kuntum"﴾ with a kasra on the alif; it is a conditional whose answer is indicated by what precedes it. The rest, al-A'raj and Qatada read ﴿"an kuntum"﴾ with a fatha on the alif, meaning: because you are. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿"idh kuntum"﴾. The "al-israf" in the verse is disbelief and far-reaching misguidance in worshipping other than Allah the Exalted and associating partners with Him.

His saying, ﴿And how many a prophet We sent among the former peoples﴾: the verses are a consolation to Muhammad (ﷺ), his mention is an example for him, a warning for them, and a threat that they will be struck by what struck those who were stronger than them in might. "al-Awwalun" [the former] are the past nations, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud and others. The pronoun in His saying, ﴿kanu bihi yastahzi'un﴾ [they used to mock him], apparently is general, and what is meant is specific to those who mocked; otherwise there were among the former peoples those who did not mock. The pronoun in "minhum" refers to Quraysh. His saying, ﴿wa madha mathalu al-awwalin﴾ [and the example of the former peoples has passed], means: their affair and their custom passed on, and they became a lesson for the remainder of time.

His saying, ﴿And if you asked them﴾ and the verse... is the beginning of an argument against Quraysh which compels upon them a contradiction in their affair, for they acknowledge that the Creator who originated them and the heavens and the earth is Allah the Exalted, yet they worship idols and call them their gods. The required answer of Quraysh would be to say: "Allah created them." When the Exalted mentioned the meaning, the expression about Allah came as "the Exalted in Might, the All-Knowing", so that this would be a preparation for what He enumerates afterwards of His attributes, which He began to report and then cut off from the speech whose meaning He related from Quraysh.

[p-535]

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿He Who made the earth for you a cradle, and made for you therein roads, that you may be guided. And He Who sent down water from the sky in due measure, and We revived thereby a dead land. Thus you will be brought forth. And He Who created all the pairs and made for you ships and cattle on which you ride, that you may sit upon their backs, and then remember the favour of your Lord when you are seated on them, and say: "Glory be to Him Who has subjected these to us, and we could not have subdued them. And indeed, to our Lord we are returning."﴾

These are descriptions of acts, and they are blessings from God Almighty upon mankind, by which proof is established against every disbelieving polytheist who associates others with God Almighty. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Who made the earth for you﴾ is not part of the speech of those who were questioned; rather, it is the beginning of an informative statement from God Almighty. The majority of readers recited "مِهادًا" (mihādan, a bed or spread-out resting place), while Ibn Mas'ud, Talha and al-A'mash recited "مَهْدًا" (mahdan, a cradle). The meaning is one: that it is spread out and that you move about and act upon it. "Subul" means paths, and "tahtadūn" (you may be guided) means: towards your destinations, from one land to another and from one region to another. It is also possible that it means: you may be guided by reflection and consideration.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿sent down water from the sky﴾ refers to rain, by consensus. The interpreters differed over the meaning of His saying ﴿"bi-qadarin" (in due measure)﴾. One group said: its meaning is by decree and determination in eternity. Others said: the meaning is in measure sufficient for welfare, neither excessive so as to cause harm, nor scant so as to fall short, but rather a rain that brings relief, a beneficial flood. Another group said: its meaning is by estimation and precision, that is, a specific known amount. Then those who held this view differed. Some of them said: each year He sends down water in one fixed amount, so that one year does not exceed another, but it falls heavily here at one time and there at another. Others said: rather, God Almighty sends down in one year a certain estimate, and in another year a different estimate, according to what His decree has preceded, there is no god but Him.

"Anshara" means: He gave life. It is said: "nashara al-mayyit" (the dead man rose) and "anshara-hu ghayruhu" (another revived him). "Baldatan" is a collective noun, and he described it as "maytan" without a feminine pronoun, because it stands in the position of "qatar" (rain) and the like, since its feminine gender is not real. The majority read "maytan" with a sukun on the yā'. Abū Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qā' read "mayyitan" with a kasra on the yā' and a shaddah. This is the reading of 'Isa ibn 'Umar. The first is more preferred, because its wording resembles "zawwara" and "'adala", so the description of the feminine by it is good. Most of the seven readers, al-A'raj and Abū Ja'far read ﴿"kadhālika tukhrajūn" (thus you will be brought forth)﴾ with a ḍammah on the tā' and a fatḥah on the rā'. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Wathhab, 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr and 'Isa read "wa-kadhālika takhrujūn" with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the rā'.

[p-536]

"Al-azwaj" means the kinds of every thing. The "min" in His saying ﴿"min al-fulki wal-an'ām" (of the ships and cattle)﴾ is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ), because only camels are ridden from among the cattle, while mules, horses and donkeys enter into what is ridden by implication. The "lām" in His saying ﴿"li-tastawū 'alā ẓuhūrihi" (that you may sit upon their backs)﴾ is the lām of command (lām al-amr), and it is possible that it is the lām of purpose (lām kay). The "mā" in His saying ﴿"mā tarkabūn" (on which you ride)﴾ refers to the type that is ridden, and the pronoun in "ẓuhūrihi" (their backs) refers to the type to which "mā" refers. Another verse has explained what is said upon boarding a ship, namely: ﴿"In the name of God is its sailing and its anchoring. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful"﴾ [Hud: 41]. This applies specifically to what is ridden of animals. What is said upon dismounting from them is: "O God, cause us to alight in a blessed place, and You are the best of those who cause to alight."

And Ṭāwūs, when he rode, would say: "O God, this is from Your bounty and Your grace," and then he would say: ﴿Glory be to Him who﴾, the verse.

[p-537]

If he sings well, well and good; otherwise, say to him: Wish for him." So he wishes for falsehoods and passes his time with that.

The Exalted and Majestic said:

"Subul" means paths, and "tahtadūn" (you may be guided) means: towards your destinations, from one land to another and from one region to another. It is also possible that it means: you may be guided by reflection and consideration.

Another group said: its meaning is by estimation and precision, that is, a specific known amount. Then those who held this view differed. Some of them said: each year He sends down water in one fixed amount, so that one year does not exceed another, but it falls heavily here at one time and there at another. Others said: rather, God Almighty sends down in one year a certain estimate, and in another year a different estimate, according to what His decree has preceded, there is no god but Him.

The Almighty said:

﴿And they have made for Him a portion from His servants. Indeed, mankind is a manifest ingrate.﴾ ﴿Has He taken daughters from what He creates and chosen sons for you?﴾ ﴿And when one of them is given good news of what he attributes to the Most Merciful, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ ﴿Is one who is raised among ornaments, and who in dispute is not clear?﴾ ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned.﴾

The pronoun in "jaʿalū" (they made) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, and the pronoun in "lahu" (for Him) refers to Allah, exalted is He. "Al-juzʾ" (portion) means a piece of a thing, a part of the whole. So it is as though they made a part of His servants a share and a portion for Him. This is the view of Mujahid and many of the commentators, and it is the saying of the Arabs: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Some lexicographers said: "Al-juzʾ" means females, as it is said: "The woman gave birth to a female" (ajzaʾat al-mraʾa), and from this is the words of the poet:

"If a free woman gives birth to a female one day, there is no wonder, for a free woman sometimes gives birth to males."

It has been said that this verse is fabricated. Qatada said: the intended meaning of "al-juzʾ" is the idols, Pharaoh, and others who were worshipped besides Allah, that is, a rival portion (juzʾan nidd). According to this view, the rebuke of the disbelievers is in two parts: concerning the idols, and concerning the angels. His saying, exalted is He, "Indeed, mankind is a manifest ingrate," uses the general word for the species, while the intended meaning is some of mankind, namely those who make this attribution and those like them. The word "mubīn" (manifest) in this verse is intransitive.

His saying, exalted is He, "Has He taken," is a rhetorical turning away (iḍrāb) and a confirmation, and this is a decisive argument against them, since the praiseworthy among children and the beloved are those whom Allah, exalted is He, has granted to the children of Adam. So how would He take for Himself the lesser share? "Aṣfākum" (chose for you) means He singled you out and made that a choice portion for you.

Then the argument was established against them in this matter by His saying, exalted is He, "And when one of them is given good news," and the verse continues. "Muswaddan" (darkened) is the predicate of "ẓalla" (became). "Al-kaẓīm" is one who is full of anger, who has swallowed his anger back into his inside, so he gulps it down and tries to hold it back, and this is perceptible at the time of anger. Then He increased their reproach and the corruption of their opinion by His saying, exalted is He, "Is one who is raised..." The word "man" (one who) is in the accusative position, governed by a verb implied by "jaʿalū" (they made), as if He said: "Or do they make one who is raised among ornaments, and who is the one you have attributed to Allah, exalted is He?" and similar to this. The intended meaning of "man" is women. This is what Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi said. "Yunashsha'" (is raised) means that she grows up and matures. The majority of reciters (qurrāʾ) read "yanshaʾu" with a fatha on the yāʾ and a sukūn on the nūn. Ibn ʿAbbas read "yunshaʾu" with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a sukūn on the nūn, making the verb transitive by the hamza. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Ḥafṣ, read "yunashsha'" with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, a fatḥa on the nūn, and a shadda on the shīn, making it transitive by intensification. This is also the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḥasan, and Mujahid. In the Mushaf of Ibn Masʿūd: "Or one who is not raised except among ornaments." "Al-ḥilya" (ornaments) means jewelry of gold, silver, and gemstones. "Al-khiṣām" (dispute) means argumentation and the pulling back and forth of debate. You rarely find a woman who does not spoil speech and mix up meanings. In the Mushaf of Ibn Masʿūd: "And he, in speech, is not clearly expressing," and "mubīn" in this verse is transitive, and the implied meaning is: not clearly expressing an aim or a point, or something similar. Ibn Zayd said: the intended meaning of "one who is raised among ornaments" in this verse is the idols and images, because they used to make many of them from gold and silver, and they would place jewelry upon many of them.

When their rebuke for what they said concerning Allah, exalted is He, by their saying "the angels are the daughters of Allah, glory be to Him," was complete, Allah, exalted is He, clarified the corruption of their statement and specified it by another aspect of corruption. That is the abominable nature of their saying about the servants of Allah, exalted is He, who are specially chosen and brought near: "that they are females." Most of the seven readers, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn Jubayr, and ʿAlqama read "ʿibādu al-Raḥmān ināthan" (the servants of the Most Merciful, females). Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Abū Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj, Shayba, Qatada, and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, read "ʿinda al-Raḥmān ināthan" (with the Most Merciful, females). This reading more clearly indicates the elevation of rank and nearness in honour, as it is said: "a near king" (malik muqarrab). Both meanings occur in the Book of Allah, exalted is He, in describing the angels in other places. He said: "Rather, they are honoured servants" (Al-Anbiyāʾ 26), and He, glory be to Him, said elsewhere: "Indeed, those who are with your Lord" (Al-Aʿrāf 206). In the Mushaf of Ibn Masʿūd: "And the angels were made the servants of the Most Merciful, females."

Nāfiʿ alone read "a-ashhidū" with two hamzas, without a madd between them, with a fatḥa on the first and a ḍamma on the second, making the second easy, between a hamza and a wāw. al-Mufaḍḍal narrated it from ʿĀṣim with the two hamzas made clear. al-Musayyibī narrated from Nāfiʿ with a madd between the two hamzas. This is the reading of al-Zuhrī, and it is a description of the females, meaning: "Did they witness their creation?" The meaning of the verse is rebuke, revealing the corruption of their minds, and their claim, and that it is stripped of proof. This is similar to the verse that refutes the astrologers and the people of natures, in His saying, exalted is He: "I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth" (Al-Kahf 51).

This is the view of Mujahid and many of the commentators, and it is the saying of the Arabs: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Some lexicographers said: "Al-juzʾ" means females, as it is said: "The woman gave birth to a female" (ajzaʾat al-mraʾa), and from this is the words of the poet:

"If a free woman gives birth to a female one day, there is no wonder, for a free woman sometimes gives birth to males."

It has been said that this verse is fabricated. Qatada said: the intended meaning of "al-juzʾ" is the idols, Pharaoh, and others who were worshipped besides Allah, that is, a rival portion (juzʾan nidd). According to this view, the rebuke of the disbelievers is in two parts: concerning the idols, and concerning the angels. His saying, exalted is He, "Indeed, mankind is a manifest ingrate," uses the general word for the species, while the intended meaning is some of mankind, namely those who make this attribution and those like them. The word "mubīn" (manifest) in this verse is intransitive.

His saying, exalted is He, "Has He taken," is a rhetorical turning away (iḍrāb) and a confirmation, and this is a decisive argument against them, since the praiseworthy among children and the beloved are those whom Allah, exalted is He, has granted to the children of Adam. So how would He take for Himself the lesser share? "Aṣfākum" (chose for you) means He singled you out and made that a choice portion for you.

Then the argument was established against them in this matter by His saying, exalted is He, "And when one of them is given good news," and the verse continues. "Muswaddan" (darkened) is the predicate of "ẓalla" (became). "Al-kaẓīm" is one who is full of anger, who has swallowed his anger back into his inside, so he gulps it down and tries to hold it back, and this is perceptible at the time of anger. Then He increased their reproach and the corruption of their opinion by His saying, exalted is He, "Is one who is raised..." The word "man" (one who) is in the accusative position, governed by a verb implied by "jaʿalū" (they made), as if He said: "Or do they make one who is raised among ornaments, and who is the one you have attributed to Allah, exalted is He?" and similar to this. The intended meaning of "man" is women. This is what Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi said. "Yunashsha'" (is raised) means that she grows up and matures. The majority of reciters (qurrāʾ) read "yanshaʾu" with a fatha on the yāʾ and a sukūn on the nūn. Ibn ʿAbbas read "yunshaʾu" with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a sukūn on the nūn, making the verb transitive by the hamza. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Ḥafṣ, read "yunashsha'" with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, a fatḥa on the nūn, and a shadda on the shīn, making it transitive by intensification. This is also the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḥasan, and Mujahid. In the Mushaf of Ibn Masʿūd: "Or one who is not raised except among ornaments." "Al-ḥilya" (ornaments) means jewelry of gold, silver, and gemstones. "Al-khiṣām" (dispute) means argumentation and the pulling back and forth of debate. You rarely find a woman who does not spoil speech and mix up meanings. In the Mushaf of Ibn Masʿūd: "And he, in speech, is not clearly expressing," and "mubīn" in this verse is transitive, and the implied meaning is: not clearly expressing an aim or a point, or something similar. Ibn Zayd said: the intended meaning of "one who is raised among ornaments" in this verse is the idols and images, because they used to make many of them from gold and silver, and they would place jewelry upon many of them.

When their rebuke for what they said concerning Allah, exalted is He, by their saying "the angels are the daughters of Allah, glory be to Him," was complete, Allah, exalted is He, clarified the corruption of their statement and specified it by another aspect of corruption. That is the abominable nature of their saying about the servants of Allah, exalted is He, who are specially chosen and brought near: "that they are females." Most of the seven readers, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn Jubayr, and ʿAlqama read "ʿibādu al-Raḥmān ināthan" (the servants of the Most Merciful, females). Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Abū Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj, Shayba, Qatada, and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, read "ʿinda al-Raḥmān ināthan" (with the Most Merciful, females). This reading more clearly indicates the elevation of rank and nearness in honour, as it is said: "a near king" (malik muqarrab). Both meanings occur in the Book of Allah, exalted is He, in describing the angels in other places. He said: "Rather, they are honoured servants" (Al-Anbiyāʾ 26), and He, glory be to Him, said elsewhere: "Indeed, those who are with your Lord" (Al-Aʿrāf 206). In the Mushaf of Ibn Masʿūd: "And the angels were made the servants of the Most Merciful, females."

Nāfiʿ alone read "a-ashhidū" with two hamzas, without a madd between them, with a fatḥa on the first and a ḍamma on the second, making the second easy, between a hamza and a wāw. al-Mufaḍḍal narrated it from ʿĀṣim with the two hamzas made clear. al-Musayyibī narrated from Nāfiʿ with a madd between the two hamzas. Abū ʿAmr, Nāfiʿ also, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Mujahid read "a-wushhidū" with the second hamza made easy, without a madd. A group of reciters read the second with easing and a madd between them. Others read "ushhidū" with a single hamza, without interrogation. This is the reading of al-Zuhrī, and it is a description of the females, meaning: "Did they witness their creation?" The meaning of the verse is rebuke, revealing the corruption of their minds, and their claim, and that it is stripped of proof. This is similar to the verse that refutes the astrologers and the people of natures, in His saying, exalted is He: "I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth" (Al-Kahf 51).

That is not from testimony that carries the meanings that are required to be fulfilled.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 43, verses 20–25:

The verse of Allah, the Exalted:

﴿They say, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of that. They only guess.﴾ ﴿Have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ ﴿Rather, they say, "We found our fathers following a community, and we are guided by their footsteps."﴾ ﴿And so We did not send a warner before you to any town but its affluent ones said, "We found our fathers following a community, and we follow in their footsteps."﴾ ﴿He said, "Even if I brought you better guidance than what you found your fathers following?" They said, "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with."﴾ ﴿So We took vengeance on them. Look, then, at the end of those who denied.﴾

Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned the disbelievers' argument from their own creeds in order to show the corruption of their position. They took Allah's granting them respite and His bounties upon them, while they were worshipping idols, as proof that He is pleased with the worship of idols as a religion. That is like a command to do so. Allah denied that the disbelievers have any knowledge of this, and there is no revealed Book with them that requires it. They only assume, conjecture and guess, and this is what is meant by *kharṣ* (guessing) and *takharruṣ* (making baseless conjectures).

Most of the reciters read *ʿalā ummatin* with a *ḍamma* on the hamza (ʿalā ummatin, "a community"). *Ummah* here means the religious path and creed (*milla* and *diyāna*). On this reading, the verse censures them for blind imitation (*taqlīd*). Mujāhid, al-Jaḥdarī and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (may Allah be pleased with him) read *ʿalā immatin* with a *kasra* on the hamza, and *imma* in this sense means blessing (*niʿma*). From this usage is the verse of al-Aʿshā:

"Nor the king al-Nuʿmān, on the day I met him, in his blessing gives gifts and is generous."

And from it is the verse of ʿAdiyy ibn Zayd:

"Then, after success, and kingship, and blessing, the graves have taken them."

On this meaning, the verse continues their argument, because they say: "We found our fathers in a blessing from Allah, the Exalted, while they were worshipping idols. That is a sign of His approval of them, and in the same way we are guided by their footsteps through this." al-Ṭabarī reports from some people that *imma* means a way or path, from your saying *amamtu kadhā immatan* (I aimed at such-and-such a way).

Then Allah, the Exalted, set an example for His Prophet ﷺ and made for him a model in those among the warners and messengers who came before him, peace be upon them. The affluent among their peoples, who were the people of blessings and wealth, had met them with this very same response.

The reciters read *qul awa law* ("Say, 'Even if...'") and that is the reading of most of the reciters. The meaning is: We said to the warner, "Say, 'Even if...'". Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥafṣ, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, read *qāla awa law* ("He said, 'Even if...'"), so in *qāla* there is a pronoun referring back to the warner. (p-542)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 43, verses 26–30:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free of what you worship,﴾ ﴿except He who originated me, for indeed He will guide me."﴾ ﴿And he made it a word that remains among his descendants, that they might return.﴾ ﴿Rather, I gave enjoyment to these people and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger.﴾ ﴿But when the truth came to them, they said, "This is magic, and indeed we are disbelievers in it."﴾

The meaning: "Remember when Abraham said..." When God, exalted is He, cited the warners (al-nudhur) as an example for Muhammad (ﷺ) and made them a model for him, He singled out Abraham, peace be upon him, for mention because of the greatness of his station. He reminded Muhammad (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, of Abraham's disavowal of his people, meaning: "So do you likewise, and bear with his steadfastness."

"Barā'" (free of, innocent of) is a descriptive adjective that applies to the singular, dual and plural, like ʿadl (just) and zūr (false). Most readers recited it as "barā'" with a fatḥah on the bā'. A group recited it as "burā'" with a ḍammah on the bā'. In the Muṣḥaf of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd) and in the reading of al-A'mash, it is "innī" with a single nūn and "barī'" (free). Al-Farrā' said: "Some people write the hamzah of the softened form as an alif in every position, without regard to the vowel before it." He said: "So perhaps the script of the Muṣḥaf of ʿAbd Allah had an alif, as in the Muṣḥaf of the community, but he pronounced it with a kasrah on the rā'."

As for His saying, ﴿except He who originated me﴾, one group said: the exception is continuous (istithnāʾ muttaṣil, an exception of the same kind as what precedes it), and they used to know God and revere Him, but they associated their idols with Him. So it is as if Abraham, peace be upon him, said to them: "I will not agree with you except in worshipping God, the Originator." Another group said: the exception is disconnected (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ, an exception not of the same kind), and the meaning is: "But He who originated me is my object of worship." On this view, they did not worship God at all, neither a little nor a lot. Abraham, peace be upon him, gave his people a reason for his worship of God, the Mighty and Majestic: that He is the one who guides and rescues from punishment. In this there is an invitation for them, an encouragement toward God, the Mighty and Majestic, and an enticement with His mercy.

The pronoun in His saying, ﴿and he made it﴾ (wa-jaʿalahā): one group said it refers to his word of tawḥīd in His saying, ﴿indeed, I am free﴾ (p. 543). Mujāhid, Qatādah and al-Suddī said it refers to what is meant by it: "There is no god but God." The pronoun returns to it although no mention of it has preceded, because the wording includes it. Ibn Zayd said what is meant by it is Islam and its word. This is supported by His, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿and from our offspring a Muslim community for You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128], and His saying: ﴿when his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131], and His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿He named you Muslims before [this]﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 78]. "Al-ʿaqib" (descendants) means the offspring, and the descendants of descendants, for as long as their branch extends.

As for His saying, ﴿Rather, I gave enjoyment﴾ and what follows, it is a statement connected to what precedes it. Because He, exalted is He, said ﴿among his descendants﴾, and the Quraysh were among his descendants, the speech required that it be understood as: "But these people are not among those in whom the word remained. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 43, verse 31–35:

His the Exalted and Majestic's saying:

﴿They say, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?"﴾ ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord? We have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and We have raised some of them above others in degrees, so that some of them may take others in service. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.﴾ ﴿And were it not that mankind would be one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses, and staircases (on which they ascend),﴾ ﴿and doors for their houses and couches upon which they recline,﴾ ﴿and adornment. And all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world. And the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous.﴾

(p-544) The pronoun in "qālū" (they said) refers to the Quraysh, because they first deemed it improbable that God the Exalted would send a human (bashar) as a messenger. When the matter of Moses, Jesus and Abraham, peace be upon them, was established, and they had no means of rejecting it, they reverted to contesting what specifically concerned Muhammad ﷺ, saying: "Why was Muhammad, peace be upon him, (chosen), when the revelation of the Law was not sent down upon a great man from one of the two groups?" Al-Mubarrad estimated their saying as: "upon a man from two men of the two cities." The two cities are Makkah and al-Ta'if. The man of Makkah to whom they pointed was, according to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi; Mujahid said he was 'Utba ibn Rabi'a; Qatada said: "It has reached us that no clan of the Quraysh remained without claiming him." The man of al-Ta'if, Qatada said, was 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud; Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said he was Habib ibn 'Abd ibn 'Umayr; Mujahid said he was Kinana ibn 'Abd Yalil.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

They only intended those whose mention was great by virtue of age and seniority. Otherwise, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at that time was greater than these, but since those were held in high esteem before the Prophet's ﷺ time and during his youth, that estimation continued for them.

Then the Exalted, in a manner of reproach to them, halted with His saying: ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ The meaning: Do the virtues and status with Allah the Exalted get divided according to their choice and will? "Mercy" (raḥma) is a term that encompasses all of this. Then the Exalted informed, with a definitive statement, that He is the one who apportions livelihoods and ranks in this world, so that some people may take others in service. The meaning: If our concern for them is to apportion this base, perishing thing, then it is more fitting that We apportion the more important and weighty matter. In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We have apportioned among them their livelihood﴾ there is a discouragement of envy and an aid to reliance upon Allah the Exalted. How excellent is the saying of the poet:

"When 'We have apportioned among them' came, disputation ceased."

al-Jumhur read "maʿīshatuhum" (their livelihood); Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read "maʿāyishuhum" (their livelihoods). Most of the people read "sukhriyyan" with a ḍamma on the sīn; Abu Raja' and Ibn Muhaysin read "sikhriyyan" with a kasra on the sīn. These are two dialectal forms with the meaning of "taskhīr" (subjugation/employment), and there is no room for the meaning of mockery in this verse.

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾ — Qatada and al-Suddi said: it means Paradise. (p-545)

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no doubt that Paradise is the ultimate goal, and the mercy of Allah, blessed and exalted, in this world through guidance and faith is better than all wealth. This wording is a belittling of this world. Then the discourse continued in belittling it with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And were it not that mankind would be one community﴾ and the rest of the verse. The meaning of the verse is that Allah the Exalted showed forbearance toward His servants and favored them by considering the preservation of goodness and faith, and willed to preserve it among a group of them for the remainder of time. Were it not for His aversion that people would all be disbelievers and people of love for this world and attachment to it, Allah the Exalted would have expanded upon the disbelievers to the utmost extent of expansion and empowered them with the world, since its insignificance in His sight requires that, for it has no worth or weight, and it is perishing and its traces vanish. So His saying: ﴿one community﴾ means: in disbelief; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Suddi. From this meaning is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "If the world were worth the wing of a mosquito in the sight of Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a drink of water from it." Then the meaning of the verse is composed upon the meaning of this hadith. The lām in His saying: ﴿for those who disbelieve﴾ is the lām of ownership; the lām in His saying: ﴿"for their houses"﴾ is the lām of specification, as you say: "This cloak is for Zayd for his mount," meaning: it is a saddle-cloth for his mount, and it belongs to Zayd as property. Al-Mahdawi said: this verse indicates that the roof belongs to the owner of the lower house, since it is attributed to the houses.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak understanding of jurisprudence.

The majority of reciters read "suqufan" with a ḍamma on the sīn and the qāf; Mujahid read "suqfan" with a ḍamma on the sīn and sukūn on the qāf; these are both plural forms. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.﴾ ﴿And were it not that mankind would be one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses, and staircases (on which they ascend),﴾ ﴿and doors for their houses and couches upon which they recline,﴾ ﴿and adornment. And all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world. And the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous.﴾

(p-544) The pronoun in "qālū" (they said) refers to the Quraysh, because they first deemed it improbable that God the Exalted would send a human (bashar) as a messenger. When the matter of Moses, Jesus and Abraham, peace be upon them, was established, and they had no means of rejecting it, they reverted to contesting what specifically concerned Muhammad ﷺ, saying: "Why was Muhammad, peace be upon him, (chosen), when the revelation of the Law was not sent down upon a great man from one of the two groups?" Al-Mubarrad estimated their saying as: "upon a man from two men of the two cities." The two cities are Makkah and al-Ta'if. The man of Makkah to whom they pointed was, according to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi; Mujahid said he was 'Utba ibn Rabi'a; Qatada said: "It has reached us that no clan of the Quraysh remained without claiming him." The man of al-Ta'if, Qatada said, was 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud; Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said he was Habib ibn 'Abd ibn 'Umayr; Mujahid said he was Kinana ibn 'Abd Yalil.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

They only intended those whose mention was great by virtue of age and seniority. Otherwise, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at that time was greater than these, but since those were held in high esteem before the Prophet's ﷺ time and during his youth, that estimation continued for them.

Then the Exalted, in a manner of reproach to them, halted with His saying: ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ The meaning: Do the virtues and status with Allah the Exalted get divided according to their choice and will? "Mercy" (raḥma) is a term that encompasses all of this. Then the Exalted informed, with a definitive statement, that He is the one who apportions livelihoods and ranks in this world, so that some people may take others in service. The meaning: If our concern for them is to apportion this base, perishing thing, then it is more fitting that We apportion the more important and weighty matter. In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We have apportioned among them their livelihood﴾ there is a discouragement of envy and an aid to reliance upon Allah the Exalted. How excellent is the saying of the poet:

"When 'We have apportioned among them' came, disputation ceased."

al-Jumhur read "maʿīshatuhum" (their livelihood); Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read "maʿāyishuhum" (their livelihoods). Most of the people read "sukhriyyan" with a ḍamma on the sīn; Abu Raja' and Ibn Muhaysin read "sikhriyyan" with a kasra on the sīn. These are two dialectal forms with the meaning of "taskhīr" (subjugation/employment), and there is no room for the meaning of mockery in this verse.

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾ — Qatada and al-Suddi said: it means Paradise. (p-545)

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no doubt that Paradise is the ultimate goal, and the mercy of Allah, blessed and exalted, in this world through guidance and faith is better than all wealth. This wording is a belittling of this world. Then the discourse continued in belittling it with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And were it not that mankind would be one community﴾ and the rest of the verse. The meaning of the verse is that Allah the Exalted showed forbearance toward His servants and favored them by considering the preservation of goodness and faith, and willed to preserve it among a group of them for the remainder of time. Were it not for His aversion that people would all be disbelievers and people of love for this world and attachment to it, Allah the Exalted would have expanded upon the disbelievers to the utmost extent of expansion and empowered them with the world, since its insignificance in His sight requires that, for it has no worth or weight, and it is perishing and its traces vanish. So His saying: ﴿one community﴾ means: in disbelief; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Suddi. From this meaning is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "If the world were worth the wing of a mosquito in the sight of Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a drink of water from it." Then the meaning of the verse is composed upon the meaning of this hadith. The lām in His saying: ﴿for those who disbelieve﴾ is the lām of ownership; the lām in His saying: ﴿"for their houses"﴾ is the lām of specification, as you say: "This cloak is for Zayd for his mount," meaning: it is a saddle-cloth for his mount, and it belongs to Zayd as property. Al-Mahdawi said: this verse indicates that the roof belongs to the owner of the lower house, since it is attributed to the houses.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak understanding of jurisprudence.

The majority of reciters read "suqufan" with a ḍamma on the sīn and the qāf; Mujahid read "suqfan" with a ḍamma on the sīn and sukūn on the qāf; these are both plural forms. Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read "saqfan" with a fatḥa on the sīn and sukūn on the qāf, as a singular. "al-Ma'ārij" are the staircases by which one ascends, so said Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and the people. Talha read "wa-ma'ārīja" with an added yā'. "Yaẓharūn" means "ya'lūn" (they ascend), and from it is the hadith of 'Aisha, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with her: "The sun was in her chamber before it rose (taẓhar)." (p-546) "Al-Sururu" is the plural of "sarīr" (couch). People differed regarding "al-zukhruf". Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Suddi said: "al-Zukhruf" is gold itself. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Beware of red, for it is among the most beloved adornments to Satan."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Beauty is red, and desires follow it. Ibn Zayd said: "al-Zukhruf" is the furnishing of the house and what is made for it of curtains, cushions and the like. A group said: "al-Zukhruf" is decoration, painting, carving and the like of embellishment. The evidence for this view is: ﴿until, when the earth takes its adornment and is beautified﴾ [Yunus: 24]. The majority of reciters read "wa-inna kullu dhalika lamma" with the mīm of "lammā" lightened; so "inna" is the light form of the heavy one, and the lām in "lammā" enters to distinguish between negation and affirmation. 'Asim, Hamza, Hisham (in one of the transmissions from him), al-Hasan, Talha, al-A'mash and 'Isa read "lammā" with the mīm of "lammā" doubled, so "in" is a negative particle meaning "mā", and "lammā" means "illā" (except). Sibawayh related: "I beseech you by Allah, except (lammā) you do it," and he interpreted it as "illā". In the Codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "wa-mā dhālika illā matā'u l-ḥayāti l-dunyā." Abu Raja' read "limā" with a kasra on the lām and lightened mīm, so "mā" means "alladhī" (that which), and its returning pronoun is omitted; the estimation is: "And all of that is for that which is the enjoyment of the life of this world." In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous﴾ there is a generous promise and an exhortation to piety, since in the Hereafter is the difference in stations.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 43, verses 36–39:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is his companion.﴾ ﴿And indeed they (the devils) bar them from the path, while they think that they are guided.﴾ ﴿Until, when he comes to Us, he says: "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts! How evil a companion!"﴾ ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you did wrong, that you are, in the punishment, sharing (it).﴾

"Man" (مَن) in His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿وَمَن يَعْشُ﴾ is conditional. "ʿashā yaʿshū" (عَشا يَعْشُو) means the sight becomes weak, like one who suffers from it at night, and thus the one who is a-ʿshā (أعشى, night-blind) among men. It is said: "ʿashā al-rajulu yaʿshū ʿashwan" when his sight is corrupted so that he does not see, or sees only a little. Qatada and Yahya ibn Sallam al-Basri read "wa man yaʿish" with a fatha on the shin (شين), which comes from their saying ʿashiya yaʿshā. The more common form is ʿashā yaʿshū, and from it is the poet's saying:

"When you come to him, groping toward the light of his fire, you will find the best fire, and with it the best hearth."

And in another poem:

"…… you will find firewood, thick and blazing embers."

Al-A'mash read "wa man yaʿshu ʿan al-Raḥmān," with "dhikr" dropped. So the meaning in the verse is: whoever his sight diminishes in regard to God's law and closes his eyelids against looking into the remembrance of the Most Merciful, that is, into what He reminded His servants of. The verbal noun is then attributed to the agent. ﴿We appoint for him a devil﴾, that is, We make it easy for him. This is the punishment for disbelief, by decree and by the absence of success. This is like the saying that God punishes disobedience by an increase in disobedience, and rewards good deeds by an increase in good deeds. This meaning has been transmitted as a prophetic report (marfu'). The majority read "nuqayyiḍ" with nūn. ʿĀṣim, al-A'mash and Abu ʿAmr (with a variant from him) read "yuqayyiḍ" with yā', "shayṭānan," that is, God appoints. Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with them both) read "yuqayyaḍu lahu shayṭānun," with a fatha on the second yā' and its doubling, and a damma on the nūn of "shayṭān."

The pronoun in "wa-innahum" refers to the devils, and in "yaṣudduhum" to the disbelievers. "The path" is the path of guidance and success. The pronoun in "yaḥsabūna" is for the disbelievers. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, ʿĀṣim (in the transmission of Abu Bakr), Ibn ʿĀmir, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, Qatada, al-Zuhri and al-Jahdari read "ḥattā idhā jā'ānā" in the dual, meaning the one who turns away and his companion; this was said by Saʿid al-Ḥarīrī and Qatada. Abu ʿAmr, Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Muḥaysin, al-A'raj, ʿĪsā, al-A'mash and ʿĀṣim read "jā'anā," meaning the one who turns away alone, and the subject of "qāla" is the one who turns away.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿بُعْدَ المَشْرِقَيْنِ﴾ admits three meanings. The first: that it means the distance of the east from the west, and He called them two easts, as one says "the two moons" and "the two ʿUmars," as al-Farazdaq said: "…… for us are its two moons and the rising stars." The second: that it means the place of sunrise at the longest day and its place of sunrise at the shortest day, as if He took the two extremes of the easts. The third: that it means the distance between the two easts and the two wests, and He suffices with mentioning the two easts.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿وَلَنْ يَنْفَعَكُمُ اليَوْمَ﴾ (the verse) relates a statement that will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection. It is a dreadful statement that deprives them of the spirit of consolation, because by it they are made to stand on the fact that consolation will not benefit them, owing to the enormity of the calamity, the length of the punishment and the continuance of its duration. In the world, consolation is generally a relief to every afflicted person. Do you not see the saying of al-Khansa':

"Were it not for the multitude of those weeping around me, over their brothers, I would have killed myself."

"They do not weep like my brother, but I console myself for him through consolation."

This consolation has spared her the burden of killing herself. So God, the Exalted, negates for them any benefit from consolation. In this is torment for them and despair of all good. The agent of "yanfaʿakum" is "al-ishtirāk" (sharing).

The majority of reciters read "annakum" with a fatha on the alif. Ibn ʿĀmir alone read "innakum" with a kasra on the alif. It is possible that the agent of "yanfaʿakum" is the disavowal indicated by His saying: ﴿Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts!﴾. On this reading "annakum" is in the accusative position as an object of cause, and the verse goes out to the meaning of the negation of solace.

The pronoun in "wa-innahum" refers to the devils, and in "yaṣudduhum" to the disbelievers. "The path" is the path of guidance and success. The pronoun in "yaḥsabūna" is for the disbelievers. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, ʿĀṣim (in the transmission of Abu Bakr), Ibn ʿĀmir, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, Qatada, al-Zuhri and al-Jahdari read "ḥattā idhā jā'ānā" in the dual, meaning the one who turns away and his companion; this was said by Saʿid al-Ḥarīrī and Qatada. Abu ʿAmr, Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Muḥaysin, al-A'raj, ʿĪsā, al-A'mash and ʿĀṣim read "jā'anā," meaning the one who turns away alone, and the subject of "qāla" is the one who turns away.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿بُعْدَ المَشْرِقَيْنِ﴾ admits three meanings. The first: that it means the distance of the east from the west, and He called them two easts, as one says "the two moons" and "the two ʿUmars," as al-Farazdaq said: "…… for us are its two moons and the rising stars." The second: that it means the place of sunrise at the longest day and its place of sunrise at the shortest day, as if He took the two extremes of the easts. The third: that it means the distance between the two easts and the two wests, and He suffices with mentioning the two easts.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿وَلَنْ يَنْفَعَكُمُ اليَوْمَ﴾ (the verse) relates a statement that will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection. It is a dreadful statement that deprives them of the spirit of consolation, because by it they are made to stand on the fact that consolation will not benefit them, owing to the enormity of the calamity, the length of the punishment and the continuance of its duration. In the world, consolation is generally a relief to every afflicted person. Do you not see the saying of al-Khansa':

"Were it not for the multitude of those weeping around me, over their brothers, I would have killed myself."

"They do not weep like my brother, but I console myself for him through consolation."

This consolation has spared her the burden of killing herself. So God, the Exalted, negates for them any benefit from consolation. In this is torment for them and despair of all good. The agent of "yanfaʿakum" is "al-ishtirāk" (sharing).

The majority of reciters read "annakum" with a fatha on the alif. Ibn ʿĀmir alone read "innakum" with a kasra on the alif. It is possible that the agent of "yanfaʿakum" is the disavowal indicated by His saying: ﴿Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts!﴾. On this reading "annakum" is in the accusative position as an object of cause, and the verse goes out to the meaning of the negation of solace.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 43, verses 40–45:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Will you then make the deaf hear, or guide the blind and those who are in manifest error?﴾ ﴿And if We take you away, indeed We will take vengeance upon them.﴾ ﴿Or We show you that which We have promised them, for indeed We are Able over them.﴾ ﴿So hold fast to that which has been revealed to you; indeed you are upon a straight path.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people, and you will be questioned.﴾ ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Merciful?﴾

When Allah the Exalted mentioned the state of the disbelievers in the Hereafter and what is said to them while they are in punishment, this required that souls be moved to compassion, and that every hearer look to his own self and strive for its deliverance. However, Quraysh, despite what they had heard, did not cease from their obstinacy and their aversion to the command of Allah the Exalted. So the address returned to (p-550) Muhammad (ﷺ), as consolation for him regarding them, and He likened them to the deaf and the blind, since their senses were of no benefit to them.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and those who are in manifest error﴾, by this He means Quraysh themselves. For this reason He did not say "or those who are", but came with the conjunctive waw, as if the Exalted were saying: "and these people". This is also supported by the return of the pronoun to them in His saying: ﴿indeed We will take vengeance upon them﴾, and no mention of them had occurred except in His saying: ﴿and those who are﴾ and His saying: ﴿And if We take you away﴾, the verse....It is a verse containing a threat that is certain to occur. The majority of scholars held that those threatened are the disbelievers, and that Allah the Exalted showed His Prophet (ﷺ) what He had promised them at Badr, at the Conquest, and other than that. Al-Hasan and Qatadah held that those threatened are within this nation, and that Allah the Exalted honoured His Prophet (ﷺ) by not having him take vengeance on them in his presence and during his lifetime; so the retribution fell upon them after he had departed, and that was in the tribulations that arose in the early period of Islam with the Kharijites and others. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: Allah, blessed and exalted, honoured His Prophet (ﷺ) by not having him see in his community what he would dislike, just as the Prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and upon them, saw; so the retribution came after his departure (ﷺ). It has been narrated in a hadith from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite: ﴿indeed We will take vengeance upon them﴾ and he said: 'By 'Ali ibn Abi Talib'." However, the first opinion regarding the threat to the disbelievers is more prevalent.

Then Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to hold fast to what had come to him from Allah the Exalted of revelation, recited and otherwise. Al-sirat (the path) means the way. The majority read "uhiya" with the verb in the passive form, while al-Dahhak read "uhiya" with the verb in the active form, meaning: Allah revealed.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you﴾, it may be that He, blessed and exalted, intends: indeed it is a source of honour and praise for you in this world—and "your people" in this sense means Quraysh, then the Arabs. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to present himself to the tribes, and when they said to him, 'To whom will the affair belong after you?' he would remain silent, until this verse was revealed. After that, whenever he was asked, he would say: 'To Quraysh.' The Arabs would not accept this until the Ansar (p-551) accepted it." Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This matter will remain among Quraysh as long as two of them remain." Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrated from him, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: "The affair will remain among Quraysh as long as they, when they judge, act justly; when they are asked for mercy, they show mercy; and when they make a covenant, they fulfil it. Whoever does not do so, upon him is the curse of Allah, the angels and all of mankind." Mu'awiya narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "This matter will remain among Quraysh as long as they establish the religion." It may also be that He intends: indeed it is a reminder and an admonition, and "your people", in this sense, is his whole community. This is the saying of al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and you will be questioned﴾, Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) and others said: its meaning is: about the commands and prohibitions of the Qur'an. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: its meaning is: about giving thanks for the blessing in it. The wording admits all of this and encompasses it.

The exegetes differed concerning the intended meaning of the questioning in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And ask those whom We sent﴾. One group said: He, the Exalted, intended: ask Jibril (peace be upon him). This is mentioned by al-Naqqash.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In this there is remoteness. Ibn Zayd, Ibn Jubayr and al-Zuhri said: He, the Exalted, intended: ask the messengers when you meet them on the night of the Isra'. Indeed the Prophet (ﷺ) did not ask the messengers, peace be upon them, on the night of the Isra' about this, because he (ﷺ) was more certain of conviction than that and was not in doubt. Another group said: He, the Exalted, intended: ask Me, or ask Us about those whom We sent. According to this interpretation, the preferable reading of "man arsalna" is as an interrogative, which he was commanded to ask with, as if his question would be: "O Lord, whom did You send before me of Your messengers? Did You make in their message the command to worship gods?" Then the question was related in reported meaning, and the address returned to Muhammad (ﷺ) in His saying: ﴿before you﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and 'Ata' said: He, the Exalted, intended: ask the followers of those whom We sent and the bearers of their laws, because what is understood is that there is no way to ask the messengers except by looking into their traces and their books and asking those who preserved them. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "wasal alladhina arsalna ilayhim qablaka rusuluna" [ask those to whom Our messengers were sent before you], this reading supports this meaning. Likewise His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82] is understood to mean that one asks only its people. Among what supports this meaning is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]; it is understood that the referral is only to the Book of Allah the Exalted and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), and that the dialogue in this matter is only with their followers and the preservers of the Shari'a. As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"yu'badun"﴾, the pronoun was brought out according to the rule for those who reason, out of regard for the wording "alihah" (gods).

Indeed, we will be guided."﴾ ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them, at once they broke their word.﴾

This is a verse presenting an example and a model for Muhammad (ﷺ) through Musa (peace be upon them both), and for the disbelievers of Quraysh through the people of Fir'awn and his chiefs. The signs with which Musa, peace be upon him, was sent are the nine, and other things beyond that which the narrations have related. Allah the Exalted singled out the chiefs for mention because they stand in place of all the people. Then He described them as laughing at the signs of Musa, peace be upon him, just as Quraysh used to laugh and scoff at the reports of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Then He the Exalted described the manner in which the signs were presented to them, and that they came one after another. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿except that it was greater than its companion﴾ is an expression of the intensity of its effect upon their souls, due to the freshness of the matter and its occurrence. This is because the first sign that Musa, peace be upon him, presented was the staff and the hand, and they were the greatest of his signs. Then every sign after that befell them and was magnified in their eyes for its time and grew great, because they had forgotten the one before it, as the poet said:

"Though wounds are healed, what remains is that
Whatever is most grand is fated to pass away with the lesser."

Al-Tabari held that the signs here are the proofs and clear evidences. Then he mentioned Allah's seizing them with punishment through the lice, the frogs, the blood and other things, and this is just as He seized Quraysh with the years of famine and the smoke.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And they said, "O sorcerer"﴾: it is possible that the one who said this knew the disbelief of sorcery, so his statement would be mockery while he knew the value of sorcery and the lowliness of its rank. And ﴿"indaka"﴾ (by what He has covenanted with you) would mean: in your claim and according to your saying. It is also possible that the speaker was not one of the stubborn skilled ones among them, and the term "sorcerer" is applied in one of two ways: either because sorcery was, among the common people, the knowledge of the age, so it is as if he said, "O learned one," or because this designation had already been applied to Musa, peace be upon him, at his first appearance, and this speaker carried it over into his address out of lack of precision and dullness. In that case the saying, according to this interpretation, is in earnest on the part of the speaker. And His saying ﴿Indeed, we will be guided﴾ would mean: if your supplication benefits us. This interpretation is more preferable; I mean that the speech of this speaker is attended with seriousness. Ibn 'Amir alone recited "yaayyuhu" with a dammah on the ha' only.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 43, verses 51–56:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people, saying, "O my people, does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Will you not then see?" "Or am I better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself? So why have bracelets of gold not been bestowed upon him, or why have the angels not come with him in succession?" So he made light of his people, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were a people who were defiantly disobedient." And when they angered Us, We took retribution from them and drowned them all. So We made them a precedent and an example for the later ones.﴾

The proclamation of Pharaoh may be understood to have been made by his own tongue at his assembly, and it may be understood to have been made by his ordering someone to call out among the people. The meaning of this argument with which he proclaimed is that he wished to demonstrate his superiority over Musa, peace be upon him, since he is the king of Egypt, possessor of the rivers and bounties, while Musa, peace be upon him, is obscure, destitute, with no worldly means. He said: "If the god of Musa were truly as he claims, he would not have left the matter in this state." Egypt extends from the sea of Alexandria to Aswan along the length of the Nile. The rivers he pointed to are the great canals branching out from the Nile, the greatest of which are the Alexandria canal, the Tinnis canal, the Damietta canal, and the Tulun canal.

As for his saying: ﴿Or am I better?﴾, Sibawayh said: "Am" here is the equalizing particle, and the meaning is: "Then do you not see, or do you see?" So in place of his saying "or do you see," he placed the matter that is worthy of being seen in his view, namely that he is better than Musa, peace be upon him. And "la" (not), according to this reading, is a negation. A group said: the meaning is: "Will you not see, or will you not see?" Then he restricted himself to "am" because the apparent speech indicates the omitted part, and he began his saying "I am better than him" as a statement from himself. So his saying ﴿Will you not then see?﴾, according to this reading, is equivalent to "hallā" and "lawlā" in the sense of urging. A group said: "am" here means "bal" (rather). Some people read: "Amma anā khayrun" (as transmitted by al-Farra'), and Mujahid used to pause on "am" and then begin: "Anā khayrun minhu." Qatada said: In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: "Am anā khayrun am hādhā."

"Mahin" means weak. His saying ﴿and can hardly express himself﴾ points to what remained in the tongue of Musa, peace be upon him, from the effect of the ember, for it had caused a knot in his tongue. When he prayed that it be loosened so that his speech might be understood, his supplication was answered, but a trace remained, so that clear expression still occurred with difficulty from him. Pharaoh reproached him with this. His saying ﴿"yakādu"﴾ implies that he did speak clearly. Abu Ja'far ibn 'Ali read "yubayyinu" with a fatha on the first ya.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿fa-lawlā uluqiya﴾: he means: from the sky, as an honour for him. The majority read "ulqiya" in the passive form. al-Dahhak read "alqā" with a fatha on the hamza and qaf, in the active form, with "asāwiratan" in the accusative. The majority of reciters read "asāwiratun," Hafs from 'Asim read "uswiratan," and this is the reading of al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu Raja', and Mujahid. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "asāwir," and in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads "asāwīr." It is said: suwār and iswār for what is placed on the arm of ornament. Abu Zayd related both forms, and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said it is like a metathesis (qalb). This was stated by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the people. It was the custom of men on that day to wear and adorn themselves with it. "Asāwiratun" is the plural of iswār. It may also be the plural of "uswiratun," like "aqiyatun" and "asaqi." Likewise "asāwiratun" is the plural of iswār, and the ha' in "asāwiratin" is a substitute for the omitted yā', because the plural is actually "asāwīr," as in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, so they dropped the yā' and made the ha' a substitute for it, as they said that of zanādiqa, biṭāriqa, and others. "Uswiratun" (p. 556) is the plural of siwār. His saying ﴿muqtarinīn﴾ means: they protect him, bear witness for him, and establish his argument.

Then the Exalted informed about Pharaoh that he made light of his people with this statement, meaning he sought their lightheartedness and their acceptance of his aim, so they responded to him and obeyed him in disbelief because of their wickedness and because of the corruption they were engaged in.

﴿Angered us﴾ means: made us angry, without any disagreement. Angering Allah, the Exalted, is that one does wicked deeds from which His acts appear that indicate the will of evil toward whomever He wills. Anger, according to this, is an attribute of act, and it is something that recurs. So if it means what appears of the acts, it is an attribute of act; and if it is returned to will, it is an attribute of essence. In this there is room for consideration.

The majority of reciters read "salafan" with a fatha on the sin and lam, the plural of sālif, like ḥāris and ḥaras. The salaf is the one who has preceded from the earlier nations, that is: We made them precursors for the disbelieving nations, as an admonition and an example for them to take lessons from, or so that they might fall into what they fell into. From this word is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The righteous depart as salaf (predecessors)," and his saying concerning his son Ibrahim, peace be upon them both: "We bury him beside our righteous predecessor 'Uthman ibn Maz'un." The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said. Hamid al-A'raj, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "sulufan" with a damma on the sin and lam, which is the reading of 'Abd Allah and his companions, Sa'd ibn 'Iyad, and Ibn Kathir, and it is the plural of salif. al-Tabari reported from al-Qasim ibn Ma'n that he heard the Arabs say: "A salif of the people has passed," meaning the salaf. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and Hamid al-A'raj also read "sulafan" with a damma on the sin and fatha on the lam, as if it were the plural of sulfa, in the sense of the nation and the cat. The others are those who will come from mankind until the Day of Resurrection.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 43, verses 57–62:**

The words of the Exalted:

﴿When the son of Mary is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it in derision.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Are our gods better, or is he?" They cite him to you only as a matter of contention. Indeed, they are a contentious people.﴾ ﴿He was only a servant upon whom We bestowed favour, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel.﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We could make among you angels to succeed you on the earth.﴾ ﴿And indeed, he (Jesus) is a sign of the Hour, so do not be in doubt about it, and follow Me. This is the straight path.﴾ ﴿And let not Satan avert you, for indeed he is to you a clear enemy.﴾

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others, concerning the interpretation of this verse, that when the verse ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59] was revealed, and along with it there was mention of Jesus, peace be upon him, his condition, and how he was created without a father, a group said: "Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, intends by mentioning Jesus only that we should worship him, just as the Christians worshipped Jesus, peace be upon him." This was their turning away from the one who cited him as an example. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, al-Nakha'i, Abu Raja', and Ibn Waththab read "yasuddun" (يَصُدُّونَ) with a ḍamma on the ṣād, meaning "they turn away" (ya'ridun). The rest of the readers, along with Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrima, read "yaṣiddun" (يَصِدُّونَ) with a kasra on the ṣād, meaning "they laugh" (yadhakun). This was stated by Ibn 'Abbas and others. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, rejected the ḍamma on the ṣād, and this was also reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Kisa'i said: "They are two dialects with one meaning, like "ya'rishun" (يَعْرِشُونَ) and "ya'rushun" (يَعْرُشُونَ)."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Are our gods better, or is he?"﴾ this begins a second meaning. It is that when the verse ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98] was revealed, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zib'ari and his counterparts came and said: "We will refute Muhammad. Are our gods better, or is 'Isa (Jesus)?" They knew that the answer would be that Jesus is (better). They said: "Is this verse of the fuel for us alone, or for all the nations of the disbelievers?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Rather, it is for everyone among the disbelievers, from earlier or later times." They said: "We are content that our gods be with Jesus, since he is better than them. And since he has been worshipped, he too is fuel then." Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿They cite him to you only as a matter of contention.﴾ That is: they did not put forth this example except as contention and sophistry on their part, and they forgot that Jesus, peace be upon him, was not worshipped with his own consent or will, nor did he bear any sin in that.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "a-ālihatunā" (أآلِهَتُنا) with an interrogative hamza, followed by a second hamza between-between (bayn bayn, i.e. an intermediate sound between hamza and a vowel) and then an alif. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read it with two fully pronounced hamzas, with an alif after the second. Warsh, on the authority of Nafi', read it without the interrogative: "ālihatunā" (آلِهَتُنا) in the form of a statement. Qalun, on the authority of Nafi', read "ālihatunā" with a single hamza followed by a long vowel. In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it reads: "khayrun am hadhā" (خَيْرٌ أمْ هَذا), so the pointer refers to Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. This reading is consistent with the first interpretation that we have explained. Likewise, a group among those who read "ālihatunā khayrun am huwa" said that the one intended is Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. This is the view of Qatadah. Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said that what is meant by "huwa" (هُوَ) is Jesus, peace be upon him, and this is the preferred view.

Al-jidal (الجِدالُ, disputation) among the Arabs means discourse aimed at sophistry, or at establishing a point, or at whatever speech happens to arise. Its purpose is only to defeat one's opponent outwardly, not to seek the truth itself. Abu Umamah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "No people went astray after being guided, while they were upon it, except that they were given to disputation." Then he recited: ﴿They cite him to you only as a matter of contention.﴾ Abu Umamah said: "The Prophet ﷺ saw a people disputing about the Qur'an, and he became angry until it was as if vinegar had been poured on his face, and he said: 'Do not strike the Book of Allah, one part against another. No people went astray except that they were given to disputation.'" Then Allah, Exalted is He, informed about them that they are people of quarrelling and fierce contention.

Allah, Exalted is He, informed concerning Jesus, peace be upon him, that he is a servant upon whom Allah bestowed prophethood and a lofty station, and made him an example for the Children of Israel. [And His saying: ﴿And if We willed﴾ (the verse), that is: do not be astonished that Jesus should be created without a father, for power requires that and more than that.]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We could make from among you﴾ means: "We could make in place of you." That is, if Allah, Exalted is He, willed, He could make, in place of the children of Adam, angels who would dwell on the earth and succeed the children of Adam in it. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: some of them would succeed others.

The pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And indeed, he is a sign of the Hour﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd said it refers to Jesus, peace be upon him. Another group said it refers to Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. Al-Hasan and Qatadah also said it refers to the Qur'an.
