Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 43, verses 69–73:

(p-562) His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims﴾ ﴿Enter the Garden, you and your spouses, rejoicing.﴾ ﴿Platters of gold and cups will be circulated among them, and therein is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in, and you will abide therein eternally.﴾ ﴿And that is the Garden which you have been given as an inheritance for what you used to do.﴾ ﴿For you therein is abundant fruit, from which you will eat.﴾

﴿"Those who"﴾ is an attributive description of the servants in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"O My servants"﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 68]. Then He mentioned His command to them to enter the Garden, they and their spouses. And ﴿"tuhbarun"﴾ means: you will be delighted and made joyful. Al-habra and al-hubur mean joy. And "al-akwab" are a kind of vessel like the ibriq (ewer), except that they have no handles or grips.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hafs from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read ﴿"ma tashtahihi"﴾ with the final hā' affirmed, and likewise it is in the Madinan codex and the codices of Syria. The rest of the readers, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and the majority read "ma tashtahi" with the hā' omitted, and likewise it occurs in most codices. Omitting it from the relative clause because of the length of the speech is good, and this is frequent in the revelation, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 41], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen"﴾ [an-Naml: 59], and other than these. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads "ma tashtahihi al-anfus wa taladhdhuhu al-a'yun" with the hā' in both places.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"you have been given it as an inheritance for what you used to do"﴾, the meaning is not that the deeds made it obligatory upon Allah to admit them to the Garden. Rather the meaning is that their shares of it are according to the measure of their deeds. As for entering the Garden itself, and a person being among its people, that is by the grace of Allah, exalted is He, and His guidance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 43, verses 74–81:

The Exalted said:

Then indeed, We are determined.﴾ ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations? When God, exalted is He, mentioned the condition of the people of Paradise and what would be said to them, He followed that with mention of the condition of the disbelievers regarding their eternal abiding in the Fire and their despair, so that the distinction would be made clear and the matters of which warning consists would become evident. The "criminals" in this verse are the disbelievers, as indicated by the eternal abiding and by what the wording of the verse contains, such as the address to Malik and other things. The "mublis" (one who is despairing, cut off from good), as said by Qatada and others, is the one who is distant and hopeless of goodness. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "wa-hum fiha mublisun," meaning in Jahannam.

As for His saying, ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾, meaning: We did not place punishment upon one who does not deserve it; rather, they wronged themselves by directing worship to one who does not merit it, and by placing disbelief and negligence in the side of God, exalted is He. The majority recited ﴿"kanu hum al-zalimin"﴾ with the separating pronoun (fasl), and Ibn Mas'ud recited "kanu hum al-zalimun" as a nominal sentence (mubtada' and khabar), with the clause being the predicate of "kana." Then God, exalted is He, mentioned concerning the people of the Fire that they call out to Malik, the keeper of the Fire, and they say, in the sense of a desire expressed in the form of a command: ﴿"let your Lord put an end to us"﴾, meaning: let Him cause us to die for a period, so that our punishment does not recur. The Prophet ﷺ recited on the pulpit: "Ya Malik," with the kaf, which is the reading of the majority. Ibn Mas'ud, Yahya, and al-A'mash recited "Ya Mal" with apocope (tarkhim). It was related from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, and Abu al-Darda', may God be pleased with him, transmitted it from the Prophet ﷺ. The "qada'" (decree/ending) in this verse means death, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So Musa struck him and ended his life﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]. It was related in its interpretation from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that Malik will remain a thousand years after their request; it was also said eighty years, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, said forty years. Then he will say to them: ﴿Indeed, you will remain.﴾

As for His saying, ﴿Certainly We brought you﴾ and what follows, it may be that it is from the speech of Malik to the people of the Fire, and His saying "We brought you" is in the manner in which one includes himself in the act of the chief, as when a man entrusted by his chief with a task says: "We overcame you, and we did such-and-such to you," and similar. Then Malik's speech ends at His saying: ﴿"averse,"﴾ Or it may be that His saying, exalted is He, "Certainly We brought you," is from the speech of God, exalted is He, to the Quraysh, following the narration of the disbelievers' affair with Malik; and in this is an eloquent threat and warning, in the sense of: "Look at how your condition will be." Then, according to this view, the verse connects to what follows concerning the affair of the Quraysh.

As for His saying, ﴿Or have they determined a matter﴾, it means: have they firmly decided upon some matter of their scheming and planning against Muhammad ﷺ, as they did when they gathered in the House of Assembly (Dar al-Nadwa) to plot against his like, and so on. The "am" (or) in this verse is the disjunctive (munqati'ah). His saying, ﴿"then indeed, We are determined,"﴾ means: then indeed We are the ones who firmly establish His victory and protection. And ibram (determination) means that you join two threads and then twist them with a firm twist; and al-barim is a thread that has two colors.

As for His saying, ﴿Or do they think﴾ and what follows, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: it was revealed because many of the Arabs believed that God, exalted is He, does not hear secret speech. From this is the hadith of the Thaqafi and the Qurashis whom Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, heard saying near the Ka'ba: "Does God hear us?" One of them said: "He hears if we speak aloud, and does not hear if we conceal..." — the hadith. Then they differed about the meaning of the verse after that. Al-Tabari said: this is a gentle manner of address, and similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

And His saying, in addressing the disbelievers: "Where are My partners?"

Mujahid said: the meaning is: if there were a son of God, exalted is He, in your saying, then I would be the first to worship God alone and to deny you. Here is the pause according to this interpretation, then one begins: ﴿So I am the first of the worshippers﴾, as related by Abu Hatim. *Whenever the affectionate friend wills, he will sever his companion,*
*and will, without doubt, be disdainful toward him, being unjust.*

He said: "So 'Uthman did not disdain (ya'bud) and sent for her to be returned." ﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide in the punishment of Hell forever.﴾ ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it in despair.﴾ ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And they will call, "O Malik (the keeper of Hell), let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾ ﴿Certainly We brought you the truth, but most of you were averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿Or have they determined upon a matter? Then indeed, We are determined.﴾ ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, recording.﴾ ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾

When God, exalted is He, mentioned the condition of the people of Paradise and what would be said to them, He followed that with mention of the condition of the disbelievers regarding their eternal abiding in the Fire and their despair, so that the distinction would be made clear and the matters of which warning consists would become evident. The "criminals" in this verse are the disbelievers, as indicated by the eternal abiding and by what the wording of the verse contains, such as the address to Malik and other things. The "mublis" (one who is despairing, cut off from good), as said by Qatada and others, is the one who is distant and hopeless of goodness. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "wa-hum fiha mublisun," meaning in Jahannam.

As for His saying, ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾, meaning: We did not place punishment upon one who does not deserve it; rather, they wronged themselves by directing worship to one who does not merit it, and by placing disbelief and negligence in the side of God, exalted is He. The majority recited ﴿"kanu hum al-zalimin"﴾ with the separating pronoun (fasl), and Ibn Mas'ud recited "kanu hum al-zalimun" as a nominal sentence (mubtada' and khabar), with the clause being the predicate of "kana." Then God, exalted is He, mentioned concerning the people of the Fire that they call out to Malik, the keeper of the Fire, and they say, in the sense of a desire expressed in the form of a command: ﴿"let your Lord put an end to us"﴾, meaning: let Him cause us to die for a period, so that our punishment does not recur. The Prophet ﷺ recited on the pulpit: "Ya Malik," with the kaf, which is the reading of the majority. Ibn Mas'ud, Yahya, and al-A'mash recited "Ya Mal" with apocope (tarkhim). It was related from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, and Abu al-Darda', may God be pleased with him, transmitted it from the Prophet ﷺ. The "qada'" (decree/ending) in this verse means death, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So Musa struck him and ended his life﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]. It was related in its interpretation from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that Malik will remain a thousand years after their request; it was also said eighty years, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, said forty years. Then he will say to them: ﴿Indeed, you will remain.﴾

As for His saying, ﴿Certainly We brought you﴾ and what follows, it may be that it is from the speech of Malik to the people of the Fire, and His saying "We brought you" is in the manner in which one includes himself in the act of the chief, as when a man entrusted by his chief with a task says: "We overcame you, and we did such-and-such to you," and similar. Then Malik's speech ends at His saying: ﴿"averse,"﴾ Or it may be that His saying, exalted is He, "Certainly We brought you," is from the speech of God, exalted is He, to the Quraysh, following the narration of the disbelievers' affair with Malik; and in this is an eloquent threat and warning, in the sense of: "Look at how your condition will be." Then, according to this view, the verse connects to what follows concerning the affair of the Quraysh.

As for His saying, ﴿Or have they determined a matter﴾, it means: have they firmly decided upon some matter of their scheming and planning against Muhammad ﷺ, as they did when they gathered in the House of Assembly (Dar al-Nadwa) to plot against his like, and so on. The "am" (or) in this verse is the disjunctive (munqati'ah). His saying, ﴿"then indeed, We are determined,"﴾ means: then indeed We are the ones who firmly establish His victory and protection. And ibram (determination) means that you join two threads and then twist them with a firm twist; and al-barim is a thread that has two colors.

As for His saying, ﴿Or do they think﴾ and what follows, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: it was revealed because many of the Arabs believed that God, exalted is He, does not hear secret speech. From this is the hadith of the Thaqafi and the Qurashis whom Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, heard saying near the Ka'ba: "Does God hear us?" One of them said: "He hears if we speak aloud, and does not hear if we conceal..." — the hadith. So God, exalted is He, informed in this verse that He hears — that is, perceives — the secret and the private conversation, and that His messengers, the angels who guard, record the deeds of mankind along with that, and they are prepared for recompense on the Day of Resurrection.

The exegetes differed concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾ One group said: "al-'abidin" is from 'ibadah (worship). Then they differed about the meaning of the verse after that. Qatada, al-Suddi, and al-Tabari said: the meaning is: Say to them, O Muhammad: If the Most Merciful had a son, as you claim, then I would be the first to worship on that basis; but there is nothing of that for Him, exalted and glorified is He. Al-Tabari said: this is a gentle manner of address, and similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

And His saying, in addressing the disbelievers: "Where are My partners?"

Mujahid said: the meaning is: if there were a son of God, exalted is He, in your saying, then I would be the first to worship God alone and to deny you. Qatada also said, as did Zuhayr ibn Muhammad and Ibn Zayd: "in" is negating, in the sense of "ma," so that it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "Say: there was not for the Most Merciful a son." Here is the pause according to this interpretation, then one begins: ﴿So I am the first of the worshippers﴾, as related by Abu Hatim. And a group said: "al-'abidun" are those who "'abida al-rajul" when he is disdainful and rejects something. The poet said:

*Whenever the affectionate friend wills, he will sever his companion,*
*and will, without doubt, be disdainful toward him, being unjust.*

From this is the hadith of 'Uthman and 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, concerning the stoned woman, when 'Ali said: "Her gestation and weaning are thirty months." He said: "So 'Uthman did not disdain (ya'bud) and sent for her to be returned." The meaning is: if you make a son for the Most Merciful and that is in your saying, then I am the first of those who are disdainful and reject that.

The majority read "walad" with fathah on the waw and the lam. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, and al-A'mash read "wulad" with dammah on the waw and sukun on the lam. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "awwalu al-'abidin" (with the variant "al-'abidin" in the sense of ... ) and on this meaning, Abu Hatim said: al-'abid, with kasrah on the ba', means one who is very angry. Abu 'Ubayda said: its meaning is: the first of those who deny, and the Arabs say: "'abadani haqqi," meaning "jahadani" (he denied me my right).

So God, exalted is He, informed in this verse that He hears — that is, perceives — the secret and the private conversation, and that His messengers, the angels who guard, record the deeds of mankind along with that, and they are prepared for recompense on the Day of Resurrection.

The exegetes differed concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾ One group said: "al-'abidin" is from 'ibadah (worship). Then they differed about the meaning of the verse after that. Qatada, al-Suddi, and al-Tabari said: the meaning is: Say to them, O Muhammad: If the Most Merciful had a son, as you claim, then I would be the first to worship on that basis; but there is nothing of that for Him, exalted and glorified is He. Al-Tabari said: this is a gentle manner of address, and similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

And His saying, in addressing the disbelievers: "Where are My partners?"

Mujahid said: the meaning is: if there were a son of God, exalted is He, in your saying, then I would be the first to worship God alone and to deny you. Qatada also said, as did Zuhayr ibn Muhammad and Ibn Zayd: "in" is negating, in the sense of "ma," so that it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "Say: there was not for the Most Merciful a son." Here is the pause according to this interpretation, then one begins: ﴿So I am the first of the worshippers﴾, as related by Abu Hatim. And a group said: "al-'abidun" are those who "'abida al-rajul" when he is disdainful and rejects something. The poet said:

*Whenever the affectionate friend wills, he will sever his companion,*
*and will, without doubt, be disdainful toward him, being unjust.*

From this is the hadith of 'Uthman and 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, concerning the stoned woman, when 'Ali said: "Her gestation and weaning are thirty months." He said: "So 'Uthman did not disdain (ya'bud) and sent for her to be returned." The meaning is: if you make a son for the Most Merciful and that is in your saying, then I am the first of those who are disdainful and reject that.

The majority read "walad" with fathah on the waw and the lam. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, and al-A'mash read "wulad" with dammah on the waw and sukun on the lam. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "awwalu al-'abidin" (with the variant "al-'abidin" in the sense of ... ) and on this meaning, Abu Hatim said: al-'abid, with kasrah on the ba', means one who is very angry. Abu 'Ubayda said: its meaning is: the first of those who deny, and the Arabs say: "'abadani haqqi," meaning "jahadani" (he denied me my right).

The Exalted said:

﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide in the punishment of Hell forever.﴾ ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it in despair.﴾ ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And they will call, "O Malik (the keeper of Hell), let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾ ﴿Certainly We brought you the truth, but most of you were averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿Or have they determined upon a matter? Then indeed, We are determined.﴾ ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, recording.﴾ ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾

The "criminals" in this verse are the disbelievers, as indicated by the eternal abiding and by what the wording of the verse contains, such as the address to Malik and other things. The "mublis" (one who is despairing, cut off from good), as said by Qatada and others, is the one who is distant and hopeless of goodness. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "wa-hum fiha mublisun," meaning in Jahannam.

As for His saying, ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾, meaning: We did not place punishment upon one who does not deserve it; rather, they wronged themselves by directing worship to one who does not merit it, and by placing disbelief and negligence in the side of God, exalted is He. The majority recited ﴿"kanu hum al-zalimin"﴾ with the separating pronoun (fasl), and Ibn Mas'ud recited "kanu hum al-zalimun" as a nominal sentence (mubtada' and khabar), with the clause being the predicate of "kana." Then God, exalted is He, mentioned concerning the people of the Fire that they call out to Malik, the keeper of the Fire, and they say, in the sense of a desire expressed in the form of a command: ﴿"let your Lord put an end to us"﴾, meaning: let Him cause us to die for a period, so that our punishment does not recur. The Prophet ﷺ recited on the pulpit: "Ya Malik," with the kaf, which is the reading of the majority. Ibn Mas'ud, Yahya, and al-A'mash recited "Ya Mal" with apocope (tarkhim). It was related from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, and Abu al-Darda', may God be pleased with him, transmitted it from the Prophet ﷺ. The "qada'" (decree/ending) in this verse means death, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So Musa struck him and ended his life﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]. It was related in its interpretation from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that Malik will remain a thousand years after their request; it was also said eighty years, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, said forty years. Then he will say to them: ﴿Indeed, you will remain.﴾

As for His saying, ﴿Certainly We brought you﴾ and what follows, it may be that it is from the speech of Malik to the people of the Fire, and His saying "We brought you" is in the manner in which one includes himself in the act of the chief, as when a man entrusted by his chief with a task says: "We overcame you, and we did such-and-such to you," and similar. Then Malik's speech ends at His saying: ﴿"averse,"﴾ Or it may be that His saying, exalted is He, "Certainly We brought you," is from the speech of God, exalted is He, to the Quraysh, following the narration of the disbelievers' affair with Malik; and in this is an eloquent threat and warning, in the sense of: "Look at how your condition will be." Then, according to this view, the verse connects to what follows concerning the affair of the Quraysh.

The "am" (or) in this verse is the disjunctive (munqati'ah). His saying, ﴿"then indeed, We are determined,"﴾ means: then indeed We are the ones who firmly establish His victory and protection. And ibram (determination) means that you join two threads and then twist them with a firm twist; and al-barim is a thread that has two colors.

From this is the hadith of the Thaqafi and the Qurashis whom Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, heard saying near the Ka'ba: "Does God hear us?" One of them said: "He hears if we speak aloud, and does not hear if we conceal..." — the hadith. So God, exalted is He, informed in this verse that He hears — that is, perceives — the secret and the private conversation, and that His messengers, the angels who guard, record the deeds of mankind along with that, and they are prepared for recompense on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 43, verses 82–85:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ ﴿So leave them to plunge in vain talk and to play until they encounter their Day which they are promised.﴾ ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God in the earth, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

When He said: ﴿So I am the first of the worshippers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81], He declared the Lord, exalted is He, free from this statement which they had made. (p-566) And ﴿"Subhan"﴾ (Glory be) is a declaration of transcendence. He singled out the heavens, the earth and the Throne because they are the greatest of created things. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So leave them to plunge﴾ is a kind of truce that was left in place, and it is abrogated by the verse of the sword (naskh: abrogation). The majority read ﴿"hatta yulaqu"﴾ ("until they encounter"), while Abu Ja'far and Ibn Muhaysin read "hatta yulqu" ("until they meet"). The majority said: the day with which He threatened them is the Day of Resurrection; ‘Ikrimah and others said: it is the Day of Badr.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God in the earth﴾ is a verse of judgment concerning His greatness and an announcement of His divinity; that is, His command is executed over everything. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hakam ibn Abi al-'As, Jabir ibn Zayd, Abu al-Shaykh, Bilal ibn Abi Burda, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read: "And He is the One who is Allah in the heaven and Allah in the earth." And ﴿"al-Hakim"﴾ (the All-Wise) means: the one who has made things firm (al-muhkam).

"Tabaraka" is from tafā'ala (the reflexive/reciprocal form), from al-barakah (blessing), meaning: His blessings have increased. And ﴿to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ is a comprehensive restriction covering all perceptible existents. And ﴿the knowledge of the Hour﴾ means: the knowledge of determining its establishment and of stopping at its specification and limitation; this is what Allah has reserved for Himself the knowledge of. Otherwise, we do have knowledge of the Hour: that it is an event with terrors and certain attributes. The verbal noun in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the knowledge of the Hour﴾ is in the genitive, being annexed to the object. Most reciters read "wa-ilayhi yarji'un" with the yā' from below (third person). Nafi', 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read "wa-ilayhi turja'un" with the tā' from above, with a ḍammah. Al-Aswad and al-A'mash read "yuhsharun" with the yā' from below.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 43, verse 86–89:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And those whom they invoke besides Him have no power of intercession, except those who bear witness to the truth and they know.﴾ ﴿And if you ask them who created them, they will surely say, "Allah." Then how are they turned away?﴾ ﴿And [He has knowledge of] his saying, "O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe."﴾ ﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace," for they will soon know.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those [whom they invoke] have no power...﴾ The verse is addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ). "Those" refers to the ones who are worshipped, and the pronoun in ﴿"yad'una"﴾ (they invoke) refers to the disbelievers who worshipped other than Allah, the Exalted. So He informs that whoever worships other than Allah does not possess any intercession with Allah on the Day of Resurrection. The majority of readers read "yad'una" with a yā' from below. Ibn Waththāb read "tad'una" with a tā' from above. Then the Exalted made an exception from these reports, and people differed about the exception. Qatādah said: He excepted from those who were worshipped besides Allah: 'Īsā, 'Uzayr and the angels, peace be upon them, and the meaning is: they possess intercession by Allah enabling them to do so, since they are among those who bore witness to the truth and know it in all their states. So the exception, according to this interpretation, is *muttasil* (connected). Mujāhid and others said: He excepted from those for whom intercession is made, as if He said: these angels, 'Uzayr and 'Īsā will not intercede except for those who bore witness to the truth and know, [i.e., of tawhid]. So the exception, according to this interpretation, is *munfasil* (disconnected), as if the Exalted said: "But whoever bore witness to the truth, these will intercede for them." The first interpretation is more correct, and Allah knows best.

Then the Exalted demonstrated the proof against them from their own statements and their acknowledgment that Allah, the Exalted, is their Creator and the One who brings them into existence after non-existence. Then He made them stand (before Him) by way of affirmation and reproach by His saying: ﴿Then how are they turned away?﴾, i.e., in what direction are they being turned away?

The majority of reciters read ﴿"wa-qīlihi yā Rabbi"﴾ with a fatḥah (accusative), and it is a verbal noun like "al-qawl" (the saying), and the pronoun in it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). Makkī related an opinion that it refers to 'Īsā (peace be upon him), but this is weak. People differed about what governs it. One group said: it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with His saying: ﴿their secret and their private talk﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 80]. Another group said: the governing element is "yaktubūn" (they record), i.e., their statements, their actions and his saying. Another group said: the governing element is what is in His saying: ﴿And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 85], of the strength of the verb, i.e., and He knows his saying. His saying: ﴿And [He has knowledge of] his saying, "O my Lord"﴾ was revealed in the sense of: the complaint of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his appeal to Allah about their disbelief and their rebelliousness.

Ḥafṣ, Ḥamzah, Ibn Waththāb and al-A'mash read ﴿"wa-qīlihi yā Rabbi"﴾ with a kasrah (genitive) by coordination with "al-sā'ah" (the Hour). Al-A'raj, Abū Qilābah and Mujāhid read ﴿"wa-qīluhu yā Rabbi"﴾ with a ḍammah (nominative) as a beginning (mubtada'), and the predicate is in His saying: ﴿O my Lord, indeed these are a people who do not believe﴾, i.e., his saying this statement; or the estimate may be: "and his saying, O my Lord, is heard and accepted." So "yā Rabbi," according to this, is in the accusative position governed by "qīlihi." Abū Qilābah read "yā Rabba" with a fatḥah on the doubled bā', intending "yā Raba," according to the dialect of one who says "yā ghulāman," then he deleted the alif for lightness and to follow the orthography of the Mushaf.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So turn away from them﴾ is a truce that was abrogated by the verses of the sword. His saying: ﴿"Salām"﴾ (peace), its estimate: "And say, my affair is peace," i.e., peaceful dealing. Another group said the meaning is: "And say, Peace be upon you," by way of truce and gentleness. The abrogation has reached this peace, whether it is a greeting or an expression of truce. The majority of readers read ﴿"ya'lamūn"﴾ (they will know) with a yā'.
